system.name: Fairness in Serving Large Language Models
system.one_liner: a study defining fairness for LLM inference serving, where request cost and server capacity both vary with input/output token counts

content.subject: why servers process fewer tokens per second when requests have long prompts and many decode tokens, versus many short requests

content.key_idea: Illustrates why a server's effective throughput drops when it serves few long requests instead of many short ones, since more decode tokens serialize into longer per-request time.
content.reading_order: left pair of long bars first (prompt then many decode-token cells, bracketed 'lower throughput'), then the right group of four shorter bars ('higher throughput')

evidence: the capacity depends on the mix between input and output tokens of existing requests
If all requests have long past tokens, then the capacity is likely to be low
input tokens are processed in parallel while output tokens must be generated sequentially

summary: This background figure from a paper on fairness in LLM serving illustrates why a server's effective throughput depends on request length rather than being fixed, unlike classic fair-queuing settings. Each request is drawn as a bar split into a solid blue 'prompt' segment and an orange, cell-segmented 'decode tokens' tail, where one cell marks the time to generate one output token. On the left, two long requests each carry a long prompt and many decode-token cells, so their per-request time is high and the server processes fewer tokens overall, yielding 'lower throughput for longer requests'. On the right, four short requests with brief prompts and few decode tokens each let the server cycle through more requests per unit time, yielding 'higher throughput for shorter requests'. Because prompt tokens process in parallel while decode tokens must be generated one at a time, request mix determines a server's usable capacity.
